title: On the Nonlinearity of Learning Rate Scaling for LLM Training
claim: Under a fixed compute budget, hyperparameters can be extrapolated along either the data axis or the model-size axis to reach the target scale.
layout: 1 panel, 2D axes (D horizontal, N vertical), color-coded extrapolation paths converging on a star
description: A single 2D coordinate plot with data scale D on the horizontal axis and model size N on the vertical axis. A red star at (D_test, N_test) in the upper right is labeled 'Predict at (D_test, N_test)' with a curved arrow pointing to it. Two green dots at (α2·D_test, N_test) and (α1·D_test, N_test) lie on a green dashed horizontal line leading to the star. They are labeled as the training scale for D-axis extrapolation. Two orange dots at (D_test, α1·N_test) and (D_test, α2·N_test) lie on an orange dashed vertical line below the star. They are labeled as the training scale for N-axis extrapolation. In the lower middle, bold red text reads 'Compute Budget Constraint:' above the equation Σ_{k=1}^{K} α_k = β. The eye goes first to the red star and the colored dashed lines.
caption: Compute-constrained extrapolation: $D$-axis extrapolation uses reduced data with the full model, while $N$-axis extrapolation uses smaller models with full data, both under a fixed compute budget.
abstract: Learning-rate transfer can reduce the cost of training large language models: instead of sweeping learning rates at target scale, practitioners extrapolate from smaller runs. Existing approaches often assume that the optimal learning rate follows a log-linear scaling law in data scale and model size. We carefully examine and evaluate this scaling law. In our empirical study of GPT-2--style models from 22M to 707M parameters trained on 5B to 100B tokens, the optimal learning rate develops upward curvature at larger scales, leading to inaccurate extrapolation. We find that this curvature largely disappears when learning rates are replaced by effective learning rate (the step size in normalized weight space), and when data $D$ extrapolation is used instead of model size $N$ extrapolation. Next, we explain nonlinearity in scaling: weight-norm converges to equilibrium slower when optimal learning is small, requiring a larger step size to reduce the transient phase. Experiments with AdamH, which directly controls the effective learning rate, further support this explanation.
